questions.answer: Set a(1, 0) + b(0, 1) = \((0, 0)\). This gives \((a, b)\) = \((0, 0)\), so \(a=0\) and \(b=0\). Since the only solution is the trivial solution, the set is linearly independent.
The second vector is 2 times the first: \((2, 4)\) = 2\((1, 2)\). Therefore one vector is a scalar multiple of the other. The set is linearly dependent.
Set a(1, 0, 0) + b(0, 1, 0) + c(0, 0, 1) = \((0, 0, 0)\). This gives \((a, b, c)\) = \((0, 0, 0)\), so \(a=b=c=0\). The only solution is trivial, so the set is linearly independent.
Notice that \((2, 1, 1)\) = \((1, 1, 0)\) + \((1, 0, 1)\). Therefore one vector is a linear combination of the others. The set is linearly dependent.

questions.prompt: Use a determinant to decide whether {\((1, 2)\), \((3, 4)\)} is linearly independent in \(\mathbb R^2\).
questions.answer: Place the vectors as columns of a matrix: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\). Its determinant is \(1\cdot4\) - \(3\cdot2\) = 4 - 6 = -2. Since the determinant is non-zero, the columns are linearly independent. Therefore the set is linearly independent.

questions.prompt: Explain why any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.
questions.answer: If a set contains the zero vector, we can put coefficient 1 on the zero vector and coefficient 0 on every other vector. This gives a linear combination equal to the zero vector with at least one non-zero coefficient. Therefore the set is linearly dependent.

questions.prompt: Can four vectors in \(\mathbb R^3\) be linearly independent? Explain.
questions.answer: No. In \(\mathbb R^3\), there are only three independent coordinate directions. Any set with more than three vectors in \(\mathbb R^3\) must be linearly dependent. Therefore four vectors in \(\mathbb R^3\) cannot be linearly independent.

questions.prompt: Find a non-trivial linear relation among \((1, 2, 3)\), \((2, 4, 6)\), and \((0, 1, 0)\).
questions.answer: The second vector is 2 times the first: \((2, 4, 6)\) = 2\((1, 2, 3)\). Move all terms to one side: 2\((1, 2, 3)\) - \((2, 4, 6)\) + 0\((0, 1, 0)\) = \((0, 0, 0)\). This is a non-trivial relation because the coefficients 2 and -1 are not both zero.

questions.prompt: For which real t are \((1, t)\) and \((2, 4)\) linearly dependent?
questions.answer: Two vectors in \(\mathbb R^2\) are linearly dependent when one is a scalar multiple of the other. If \((2, 4)\) = 2\((1, t)\), then 2t = 4, so \(t=2\). Equivalently, \(\det\left(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\t&4\end{pmatrix}\right)\) = 4 - 2t, and this is zero when \(t=2\). Therefore the vectors are dependent when \(t=2\).

questions.prompt: A learner says a set is linearly independent if none of its vectors is zero. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Having no zero vector is necessary but not sufficient for linear independence. For example, \((1, 2)\) and \((2, 4)\) are both non-zero, but \((2, 4)\) = 2\((1, 2)\), so the set is linearly dependent. The learner checked only one possible cause of dependence, not all linear relations.
